summary: The three round-8 fixes are all verified good, and the cost-citation abstention is the right call for a reason stronger than the one given: R6 does exist (cost.md line 10 defines the R<n> namespace) but reads 'independent of INDEX count', and non-negotiable 6 names neither pods nor nodes on the forbidden side -- so no rule number supported the bullet, and Sequencer.commitAll's own javadoc ('M4.7's cost argument is that the commit rate scales with WINDOWS rather than pods') supports the tree fact directly. One new major, in the clause added at round 8: M4.10d justifies the checkpoint fold with a cost claim that ChainReplay.applyChain falsifies, and the same sentence contradicts itself about whether the chain holds the key. Remedy is a deletion or a one-clause correction; three minors alongside.

findings.title: The tail is neither a cost gap nor forbidden: ChainReplay already GETs every uncheckpointed entry on recovery, and M4.10b's property is scoped to the COMMIT path
findings.detail: M4.10d ends: 'Only `flushSeq` is absent from the chain: `SegmentKey` puts `podShortId` and a per-pod sequence inside the segment key that every `SegmentCommit` carries, and each `RunCommit` carries the original offsets -- so the tail is a COST gap, not an information gap, and reading it means the backwards walk M4.10b's cost property forbids.' Measured against the tree, the trailing claim is false twice over. (1) sequencer/src/main/java/binjava/sequencer/ChainReplay.java:362 `applyChain(Hop)` LISTs from `keyFor(hop.from() - 1)` and does `ChainEntry entry = read(store, stat.key())` for every entry from the seeded checkpoint's sequence up to the barrier -- and `crossFromCheckpoint` (line 234) seeds that hop from the newest SAFE checkpoint, including the PREDECESSOR's chain at takeover. So the uncheckpointed tail is already GET and decoded on every recovery; harvesting per-pod state from those same already-decoded entries adds ZERO object-store requests. (2) M4.10b's property as written is 'It must add no COMMIT-PATH request that scales with the number of pods' (line 222). Recovery is not the commit path, and cost.md R2 explicitly puts recovery outside the hot-path rule. What the property actually forbids is walking back PAST the newest checkpoint, or consulting the chain once per commit -- not reading a tail that is read anyway. The first half of the same sentence is also self-contradictory: if `flushSeq` -- the second component of the dedup key -- is absent from the chain, then a chain-only read cannot answer a `(podId, flushSeq)` replay, which is an INFORMATION gap, not a cost one. Either the segment key substitutes for `flushSeq` (then the sentence's 'only flushSeq is absent' framing is the wrong one) or it does not (then 'not an information gap' is wrong).
findings.failure_scenario: A session picks up M4.10b, reads that consulting the chain for a replay is forbidden outright, and concludes that a durable carrier is mandatory -- which routes straight into M4.10c, the row this decomposition itself calls 'POSSIBLY VOID' and the most expensive item in the split. The zero-marginal-cost option (reconstruct per-pod state from the tail entries recovery already decodes) is ruled out by a cost claim that does not hold, and the genuinely decisive constraint is never stated: the fold is needed not because the tail is expensive but because the checkpoint ABSORBS everything before it, so a replay whose original commit predates the newest checkpoint has nothing left on the chain to be read at all. The row currently gives the wrong reason for the right prescription, in the paragraph a session reads to decide whether the fold is necessary.
findings.remedy: Cheapest fix, matching round 8's pattern and adding no new claim: delete from '-- so the tail is' to the end of the sentence, leaving the two verified tree facts standing. If the test reviewer's half-clause must be served, the true one-clause form is: the tail is read anyway (`ChainReplay.applyChain`), so the fold exists for the history the checkpoint has already absorbed, which the tail by definition does not contain. Arguing it in a staged `baselines/review.txt` entry that carries the `applyChain` measurement is an equally legitimate resolution under review.md rule fixed-or-argued.

findings.title: M4.10d's stated blocker is M4.10b alone, but its refusal keys on the carrier M4.10c ships
findings.detail: Line 186 says 'M4.10d is blocked by M4.10b' and then 'how far its dedup reaches depends on M4.10b's answer: returning the original offsets across a takeover needs a carrier for `flushSeq`'. M4.10b is an ADR and ships no code; the carrier, when one is needed, is M4.10c's. Nothing in either row says d lands AFTER c whenever c is non-void, and M4.10c's own banner ('CONDITIONAL ON M4.10b AND POSSIBLY VOID. Do not start before that ADR lands.') invites a session to skip it.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.10b's ADR decides the key must be qualified with an incarnation token carried in a new field. A session reads 'M4.10d is blocked by M4.10b', sees b landed, treats c as the conditional/optional row, and builds the dedup on the only key available today -- the bare `(podId, flushSeq)`. That is precisely the failure the parent row exists to prevent: post-restart flushSeq 0 matches pre-restart flushSeq 0 and a real commit is SUPPRESSED. The suite would be green, because `CheckpointWriterContentTest`'s takeover fixture has one incarnation of `poda` and, as M4.10d itself records, 'dedup on the BARE pair passes it'.
findings.remedy: One clause on line 186: d is blocked by b, and by c whenever c is non-void.

findings.title: The 'changes no format at all' option and the 'no eviction' property are stated apart, and it is the first that makes the second bite
findings.detail: Property 2 (line 220) names the gap: 'No object may grow with history (ADR-0033), and `CheckpointWriter`'s pods map has no eviction.' The last bullet (line 233) offers the cheap answer: 'Qualifying the key inside `Checkpoint.pods`'s existing `String` changes no format at all'. The two are never connected, and the connection is the sharpest constraint on the ADR: `pods` keyed by bare `podShortId` is bounded by FLEET SIZE, but keyed by any per-incarnation qualifier it gains a key per restart and is bounded by nothing (`CheckpointWriter.java:78` is a plain `HashMap`, `Checkpoint.encode` writes one length-prefixed String plus one uvarint per entry, and `crossFromCheckpoint` GETs the whole checkpoint on every recovery).
findings.failure_scenario: An ADR takes the 'no format change' route, satisfies property 2 by reading it as ADR-0033's subject (the segment index stays out of the checkpoint), and ships a checkpoint whose pods map grows one entry per pod restart forever -- read in full on every recovery and at every takeover, which is the unbounded-read class M4.9 exists to remove.
findings.remedy: Half a clause on the last bullet, or on property 2: qualification is what converts a fleet-bounded map into a history-bounded one, so an answer that qualifies owes an eviction rule.

findings.title: The argued rounds: entry narrates through round 6 and lands at round 9
findings.detail: The entry ends 'Round 6 cuts every mechanism guess and moves the end-to-end anchor OUT of the conditional row.' Rounds 7 and 8 then found two more majors, and the round-7 one is the failure class this repo tracks hardest and records by name in the M4.9 and M0.76 entries beside it: a cost property citing a rule number that resolves to nothing in `cost.md`, in a project whose one line is the cost rule. review.md rule two-round-cap requires only a key and a reason, so the gate is satisfied -- but the entry is the permanent trace of what the extra rounds bought, and it currently understates both the count and the finding.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone later reads the rounds: list as the signal review.md says it is ('a growing list is a signal, not a workflow') and sees a six-round decomposition, not a nine-round one whose seventh round caught an invented rule citation. The evidence for the escape being used well, and the evidence of the recurring failure, are both lost.
findings.remedy: Two clauses appended to the existing line, naming the R6 citation that resolved to nothing and the retired-candidate worked example. Under review.md rule minors-land this may equally be recorded in the commit body and left alone.

verified: Cost citation (round-8 major): `grep -n 'R6' docs/internal/standards/cost.md` returns nothing literally, but cost.md:10 states 'rule 1 is R1, rule 18 is R18', so R6 DOES exist as a citation -- and it reads 'Commit/metadata write rate is independent of index count', which is the INDEX axis, not the pod axis, so it would not have supported the bullet in any case. cost.md:17 permits scaling with segments/AZs/nodes; non-negotiable 6 forbids records/shards/partitions/indices. Pods appear on neither side. Citing no rule and stating the tree fact is correct. The tree fact is better supported than the row claims: `sequencer/src/main/java/binjava/sequencer/Sequencer.java:100` says 'M4.7's cost argument is that the commit rate scales with WINDOWS rather than pods' and warns that a looping default 'would silently restore the per-pod PUT rate the milestone exists to remove'. That javadoc, not a rule number, is the text to cite if a citation is ever wanted. (Noting for the record: the landed M4.7a row DOES say non-negotiable 6 'forbids by name' the per-pod commit rate -- so it is the landed row that stretches, not this abstention.)

Worked example (round-8 major): no 'poda@e7' or any instance of a qualified key anywhere in the staged bytes. The surviving property is true as stated -- `Checkpoint.pods` is `Map<String, Long>` (Checkpoint.java:44), encode writes the key as a length-prefixed String (line 130-137), `VERSION = 0` is a constant compared once in decode, and the record's compact constructor rejects only blank keys, so a qualified key round-trips and compares equal with no format change.
Minor 'all three goldens': there is exactly one checkpoint golden, format/src/test/resources/golden/checkpoint-v0.bin (seven goldens total). Deletion correct.

Minor 'the four above' -> 'the two above': the referent is bullets 1 (answered, not detected) and 2 (no growth with history), and the claim holds -- a per-pod `ctl/pods/<podId>` object rewritten per commit satisfies both while multiplying the commit PUT rate by pod count. Correct as amended.
Minor 'nothing owning it': gone; M4.10c line 179 carries the division ('everything that needs no format change is M4.10d's').
backlog.md M4.10b row says 'Six properties in the notes' -- the notes carry exactly six bullets.

Spot-checked tree claims that survived from earlier rounds, all true: DefaultIngest.java:63 holds `flushSeq` as an instance field and line 349 is the sole issuance site, incrementing unconditionally; SegmentPublisher.java:53 is an instance AtomicLong and line 137 carries the 'unique WITHOUT coordination' phrase; SegmentKey.render takes (prefix, timestampMillis, podShortId, sequence, headerLen, filter); Checkpoint.pods is written by CheckpointWriter.java:129 (`Math::max`) and read by nothing -- crossFromCheckpoint consumes only `checkpoint.streams()`; ChainEntry has VERSION_DELTA=0 and VERSION_KINDED=1 with KIND_DELTA=0 claimed off a reservation; ChainReplay.java:441 folds `merge(run.key(), run.lastOffset() + 1, Math::max)`; Invariants.java:116 uses `delta.runs()`, which CommitDelta.only() makes throw IllegalStateException on a batch; CheckpointWriterContentTest replays 9 then 4 and carries the `doesNotContainKey("poda")` tripwire at line 156; the M3.0 quotation matches backlog-done.md:93 verbatim across the elision; BatchingSequencer is constructed only in its own three test classes.

Cost lens on the decomposition as a whole: no row prescribes a request that scales with records, shards, partitions, indices or pods. M4.10d's fold is in-memory and rides the existing checkpoint PUT; the recovered window comes from a checkpoint recovery already GETs. The one cost defect is the overstated prohibition in finding M410-r9-1, which errs toward MORE constraint, not less.
